digestIntro: Two threads dominate today and they intersect directly with your work, Midya. First, the U.S. AI policy vacuum — a shadow regulatory regime operating through ad-hoc interventions rather than clear rules — creates both risk and opportunity for Canadian institutions and consultants positioning AI responsibly.
whyItMatters: Two threads dominate today and they intersect directly with your work, Midya. First, the U.S. AI policy vacuum — a shadow regulatory regime operating through ad-hoc interventions rather than clear rules — creates both risk and opportunity for Canadian institutions and consultants positioning AI responsibly. Second, global higher-ed is reshuffling fast: the QS rankings show the U.S. losing research ground to China, the Netherlands posted its first-ever international student drop, and Quebec's English-medium universities just settled a French-language deal that reshapes the operating environment for schools like McGill and Concordia. These are live signals for your consulting pipeline. On the home front, Kamloops councillors are asking Ottawa for AI data centre guidance — a localized version of the same governance gap you see at the federal level — and the Iran ceasefire is starting to ease global oil prices, which has real downstream effects on operating costs and consumer confidence.
audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Thursday, June eighteenth, twenty twenty-six. The AI governance vacuum is the thread running through almost everything today — from the White House to Phoenix to your own backyard in Kamloops.

Let's start with AI, because there are three stories today that together form one coherent, important picture.

The first is what Axios is calling Trump's shadow AI policy. The administration came into office promising to get government out of the industry's way. It hasn't worked out that way. What's actually emerged is a patchwork of behind-the-scenes interventions — case-by-case decisions, quiet pressure, selective enforcement — that shape the AI industry's future without ever spelling out the rules. The White House says AI shouldn't be regulated, but it is, effectively, being regulated. Just not transparently, and not consistently.

Why does that matter to you specifically? Because when you're advising Canadian institutions and brands on AI strategy, the policy environment south of the border shapes what vendors, models, and partnerships are actually safe to build on. A shadow regulatory regime means unpredictable reversals. That means your advice needs to include a layer of scenario planning — what happens if the U.S. suddenly shifts posture on a particular model, a particular data practice, a particular partnership? Canadian clients need to be building on foundations that don't crack when Washington changes its mind on a Tuesday.

The second AI story is about who's actually running AI policy inside the White House right now. David Sacks, who was one of the key Silicon Valley architects of the administration's AI agenda, is stepping back from day-to-day involvement. Sriram Krishnan is preparing to leave entirely. What that means in practice is that influence over AI policy is dispersing to a broader, less coherent group of White House aides — people without the same depth of industry knowledge or consistent ideological framework. The risk is policy whiplash: moves made for political reasons rather than technological ones. For anyone building long-term AI strategy, that's a meaningful variable.

The third AI story is the one that connects most directly to your local context. Arizona has become the bellwether for what the AI data centre boom actually costs — not in dollars, but in water and power. A member of the Arizona Corporation Commission put it bluntly: what took their utilities over a hundred years to build, they now need to double within the next four to five years just to keep up with data centre demand. That's not a manageable infrastructure challenge. That's a structural crisis.

And here's why this landed in your briefing even though it's about Phoenix: Kamloops city councillors are wrestling with exactly the same question right now. They've gone on record saying municipalities lack the framework to evaluate AI data centre proposals. They're asking Ottawa for federal guidance. That's a governance gap. And it's playing out in the same city where TRU is located, where you live part of your life, and where land-use decisions are being made right now without a proper policy foundation. The Arizona story is the cautionary tale. The Kamloops story is the live situation.

Let's move to higher education, because today's stories here are genuinely consequential for your consulting pipeline.

The most operationally significant story: Quebec and English-medium universities have reached a deal on how Bill 96's French-language requirements will apply to them. This directly affects McGill, Concordia, and Bishop's. These institutions have been operating under significant uncertainty about how aggressively the language requirements would be enforced, what the implications would be for their international student recruitment, and how they'd need to restructure communications and programming. That uncertainty is now resolving. And when a major regulatory overhang lifts at a university, the leadership teams turn their attention to strategy. That's your moment. If you have any McGill or Concordia contacts, now is the time to be in their inbox — not to pitch directly, but to share a thoughtful observation about what the deal means for their enrolment and brand positioning. That's the kind of advisor move that opens doors.

Also at McGill: the Goodman Cancer Institute has formalised a research partnership with Asimov, an AI-driven biologics company. On its own, this is a science story. But read it through a consulting lens and what you see is McGill actively building industry-facing AI research partnerships — which means there are people at that institution whose job is now to integrate AI into their research enterprise. Those people need help thinking about how to communicate that work, how to attract the right partners, and how to position McGill's AI research brand externally. That's a real opening.

Beyond Canada, the QS Rankings twenty twenty-seven are out, and the headline finding is striking: U.S. universities are losing ground on research impact and international talent attraction to rivals in China and beyond. American institutions still lead on graduate employability, but the research gap is closing and the international talent race is tightening. For Canadian universities, this is an opportunity. If the U.S. brand is weakening among international students and researchers — and there's evidence it is, partly driven by visa hostility and political climate — then Canada's positioning improves by default. The institutions that move quickly to articulate that positioning clearly and compellingly will capture disproportionate share. That's a consulting thesis worth developing.

And reinforcing that point: the Netherlands just recorded its first-ever drop in international students. The Netherlands had a twenty-year unbroken streak of growth. It's over. The same pressures — visa tightening, cost of living, political messaging — that hit Canada hard in twenty twenty-four and twenty twenty-five are now hitting European destinations too. This is a global correction, not a Canada-specific problem. The institutions that read that correctly and position themselves as stable, welcoming, and high-value will recover fastest. That's the strategic frame for your higher-ed consulting conversations.

A quick note on the macro business environment, because it sets the context for every consulting conversation you're having right now.

U.S. gas prices have dropped back below four dollars a gallon for the first time in months, following an extended ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran that's beginning to reopen Strait of Hormuz shipping. The months of war-driven oil price inflation compressed consumer budgets and created a cautious spending environment that rippled through marketing budgets everywhere. The easing of that pressure is real, but analysts are clear that prices won't return to pre-war levels quickly. The mood is cautiously optimistic, not ebullient. That's the register for business conversations right now — relief, but not confidence.

Also worth noting: UK job vacancies just hit a five-year low, with companies pulling back sharply on new hiring. The UK is often a leading indicator for broader developed-economy sentiment. When businesses stop hiring, they're also tightening every other discretionary spend. If you're scoping consulting engagements with institutions that have UK or European exposure, expect longer decision cycles and more scrutiny on ROI.

On real estate, one story worth a quick scan: HousingWire released their annual roundup of the ten best real estate marketing companies for 2026. It's a useful competitive intelligence piece if you're tracking where brokerages and agents — including eXp-aligned ones — are directing their marketing spend. The vendors on that list represent the infrastructure layer of the real estate marketing ecosystem. Knowing who's gaining share and who's losing it gives you useful context for any real estate-adjacent consulting conversations.

A few local items you should know about.

Beyond the AI data centre story I already covered, there's a scam circulating in Kamloops right now: fraudulent text messages claiming to offer property tax discounts, impersonating the mayor's office. The city has officially confirmed these are not legitimate. Please make sure your family members in the area know about this — it's exactly the kind of plausible-sounding local scam that can catch people off guard.

And a genuinely positive local development: Thompson Rivers University may be in line for federal funding if Ottawa acts on a Senate report recommending investment in wildfire science and community resilience research. TRU is well-positioned to be a beneficiary, which would meaningfully strengthen its research profile and funding base. From your perspective, a TRU that's growing its federal research portfolio is also a TRU that's building new internal programs, new external partnerships, and new communications needs. Worth watching.

Two significant global stories today.

U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth went to Brussels, lashed out at NATO allies, and announced a six-month Pentagon review of American troop deployments in Europe. This is a significant escalation of the U.S.-NATO tension that's been building throughout this administration. For a senior leader tracking geopolitical risk, the practical implication is continued instability in the transatlantic alliance — which affects trade, investment flows, and the broader environment in which Canadian institutions and businesses are operating. It also accelerates European countries' push for strategic autonomy, including in technology and AI governance, which creates its own ripple effects in sectors you work in.

In Africa, gunmen attacked the main airport in Niamey, Niger's capital, this morning in a serious security incident. Niger is part of a broader pattern of security deterioration across the Sahel. This one matters at the global-awareness level — it's a signal that instability in that region is deepening, which has implications for global commodity supply chains and for the international development work that many Canadian universities and NGOs are involved in.

Two longevity stories today, both from STAT News.

The first is one you should share with family: nitazenes, a class of synthetic opioids more potent than fentanyl, are spreading rapidly across the U.S. drug supply. CDC data shows confirmed overdose deaths involving nitazenes rose from twenty-seven in 2020 to four hundred and nine in 2024. That's an order-of-magnitude increase in four years. These drugs are also appearing in the Canadian supply, and BC's overdose crisis makes this directly relevant. Nitazenes are dangerous because they often appear as adulterants in other substances and because standard naloxone dosing may be insufficient. This is worth a conversation with anyone in your family circle who might be in proximity to drug use situations.

The second longevity item: STAT News ran a status-report episode on what's next for the GLP-1 weight-loss drug market. This category — Ozempic, Wegovy, and the drugs coming after them — is now the most consequential pharmaceutical story for cardiometabolic health globally. The episode covers new entrants, access barriers, and emerging long-term use data. It's worth fifteen minutes of your time, not just as a health story, but because the GLP-1 market is reshaping insurance, employer health benefits, and the broader wellness economy in ways that touch adjacent sectors.

That's your Thursday briefing, Midya. The through-line today is governance catching up with speed — AI policy, international student flows, Quebec language rules, data centre siting. In every case, the rules are being written in real time, and the institutions and consultants who understand the direction of travel before it's codified are the ones who'll be in the room when decisions get made. You're well-positioned to be that person for your clients. Use it. Have a strong day.
